item.title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8g49e0gwxeno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks - Published Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS. The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings. The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public. "We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face." The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran. One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal. While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo, apparently of the same radar aircraft in March. The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats. At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base. A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site. Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait. Damage to the site was reported in March, including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack. Brian Katulis, a former national security official under both Democratic and Republican administrations, said that the damage visible in the images showed that "America had not adequately prepared its defences". "And there is strong evidence that US adversaries like China and Russia may have helped Iran in targeting," added Katulis, now a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. "The Trump administration has done nothing to address these vulnerabilities." The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict". It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said. In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues. The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions". A separate report , externalfrom the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7. The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b). CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports. Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report. Brian Katulis of the Middle East Institute said that while "these costs show how the Trump administration burned through precious military resources without having much to show for it", the greater damage had been to broader US military readiness. "The United States had to divert military assets from Asia to the Middle East, leaving America and its partners in Asia more exposed and vulnerable to China," he said. "In addition, the depletion of US munitions makes Russia more willing to probe vulnerabilities with America's NATO allies and continue its aggressive war against Ukraine." While the US has the financial resources to address the equipment losses, it is already facing budgetary problems and may not be able to do so fast enough to prepare for potential flare-ups in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, he added. Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country. Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel. On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval. The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matter ahead of the US midterm elections in November. It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter. The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US. The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job". - Published1 day ago

item.title: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjwyzrr9d3dko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member' - Published The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member". Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade. Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength". She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system". Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday. Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours. - Carney's new love-in with EU has everything to do with Trump - Published9 hours ago Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics. "And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy." She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation. Both she and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems. In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark. But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years. Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status. Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership. In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying. Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada. Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia. "For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address. "This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality." Calls for such a body have been growing since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It was initially a French-German conception but more countries have shown support, particularly as Trump has questioned the Nato military alliance. Other nations worry such a council could unhelpfully rival Nato. Von der Leyen said the EU was "strengthening our work with Nato" and that expanded defence spending would be "fully aligned" with the alliance. But at the core of such a security council would be the ability to trigger an emergency meeting if one member felt under threat, similar to Nato's Article 4. The EU chief said it would be a "mechanism to flank" Article 4, a term that could be interpreted as complementing Nato functions or - if taken in a military context - bypassing them. Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society. Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU. Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents. A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined. The pledge chimes with the message of European politicians on the right and hard right who have gained support in recent years for proposing a tougher approach. Some of them called the mass attempt to enter the EU through Ceuta an "invasion" and argued asylum rules should be suspended to deal with such a crisis. Von der Leyen said the new emergency tool would "only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and for a specific period of time, and that fundamental rights would be protected. Human rights groups worry such a move would see vulnerable people, including women and children, turned back and denied the protection afforded to them under international law. item.title: Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers say
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvp8d00j9gg5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Eight children among 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses, rescuers say - Published At least 21 people have been killed, including eight children, after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip overnight, rescuers and medics say. Witnesses told the BBC that the six-storey building in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa area had been left tilting dangerously to one side after an Israeli strike more than a year ago. Displaced families had lived inside because they were desperate, they said. UN and Egyptian teams joined the search for survivors, which was slow due to a lack of equipment. Initially, rescuers from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency had to use their bare hands. On Wednesday afternoon, they said they had ended the operation after taking 45 injured people to hospitals. Sherif, whose sister was killed, said: "They couldn't find a tent or somewhere to live. "This was the last place they could turn to, despite the danger. They were aware that it would likely end in tragedy. A lack of resources drove them towards certain death." A woman living in a tent nearby, Umm Mohammed Bakrun, said she had been talking to her son when the building collapsed suddenly in the early hours of Wednesday. "It felt like an earthquake. There was a loud sound and I couldn't stand up. Stones rained down on us and when I looked outside I saw a lot of dust," she told the BBC. "Within minutes, there were screams everywhere." Another witness, Mansour Abu Mohammed, said the building collapsed "in a few seconds". "Every day, a stone or a few stones would fall from it, but the people inside couldn't find anywhere else to live. I used to live next door to it and you could see that it was tilting to one side." Satellite imagery shows that the area around the building was targeted in the early weeks of the war, while damage to the building itself first became evident in 2024. The head of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Gaza office, Alessandro Mrakic, told reporters at the scene on Wednesday morning that "the situation... is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed". He also warned that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza were at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches. "We need support, most importantly with machinery, equipment, among others. Our colleagues here don't have [engine] oil and spare parts to continue to work with all the equipment that is still in Gaza." The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was "devastated" by the reports of the building collapse. "No-one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he said. He also urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries to Gaza of heavy machinery for rescue operations, as well as tents, tarpaulins and other non-food items for displaced people ahead of the winter rains. Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups that could also have military uses. An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN. More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says. The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed last October, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement. On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources. The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed. Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza. A spokesperson for the Israeli military told the BBC it was not aware of such an incident. The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage. Since then, more than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. item.title: US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62l8g8qlr0ko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US House votes to hold billionaire Epstein associate Leon Black in contempt - Published The US House of Representatives has agreed to hold billionaire Leon Black in contempt of Congress for defying legal summons related to its investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Black - who had business ties to Epstein - did not comply with a subpoena ordering him to appear before the House Oversight Committee earlier this month and share documents related to Epstein. Lawyers for Black, who has sued over the summons, called the contempt move "outrageous". After passage of the measure holding Black in contempt, Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer said: "No one is above the law." "We will continue to seek transparency for the American people and justice for survivors." In a statement shared with US media, lawyers for Black called the House move an "outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr. Black". "The full House is holding him in contempt without any regard to the active litigation challenging the lawfulness of the Committee's actions and the ethics complaint against Chairman Comer," they said. The measure, which passed by unanimous consent, means the matter will be referred to the US justice department, which will decide whether to criminally prosecute Black. In a statement, the committee's top Democrat, Congressman Robert Garcia, called the contempt vote "an important step towards justice and accountability". "We will continue to center the survivors in our fight to hold those responsible for these horrific crimes," he said. Black walked out of voluntary testimony before the House Oversight Committee in June after he was asked about nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) he may have signed, lawmakers said at the time. Black left Apollo Global Management, which he co-founded, amid scrutiny in 2021 over his Epstein ties. He has denied any wrongdoing with regards to his dealings with Epstein. The subpoenas, which ordered Black to share NDAs and give an on-camera deposition under oath, were issued after he left the committee meeting in June. Black has said he hired Epstein as a wealth management adviser, telling lawmakers in June that he gave Epstein $158m (£118m) for legitimate reasons. The billionaire has said he did not know about Epstein's crimes until he was charged with sex trafficking in July 2019. item.title: OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2zpj4y525o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
OpenAI boss says world 'right to be afraid' but should trust AI firms - Published The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks. "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco. He accepted people were justified in being concerned about AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly. But critics say firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate, with left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, among those calling for greater governance of AI. Trump himself has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax". He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president. Altman's comments on Tuesday came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce. "It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this." But AI bosses themselves have also admitted it may be difficult to regulate a technology which is changing so quickly. In an interview with Axios published on 3 September, external, Altman said he had expected Congress to create a "basic framework" for advanced AI after his 2023 testimony, but that has yet to happen. He suggested lawmakers have struggled to keep pace with the technology and to regulate it without "slow[ing] down innovation". New safety legislation on AI is unlikely to emerge from the US Congress anytime soon, despite the fact lawmakers returned from their summer break on Monday. There is a lack of consensus within both US parties on how any regulation would happen - and the House is set to enter recess again at the end of the week ahead of the midterm elections in early November. - Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings - Published12 hours ago Altman's comments on Tuesday were the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked. A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing. After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, external that every AI firm had the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards safety. "Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," the Meta chief executive wrote. "Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well." Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value. Some political figures have pushed back against the view that AI firms should be able to self-regulate. Bernie Sanders said decisions about AI had been left to "a handful of the richest people in the world", while former White House strategist Steve Bannon said the public could not trust tech oligarchs to regulate themselves. Nvidia boss Jensen Huang said at the same conference on Tuesday that AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released - and not be managed by outside forces. "We don't need new laws or regulations," he said, adding there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products. Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for its hardware. Huang also argued safety is an "engineering problem" and companies should "take a pause" if they lose confidence in a product. The recent claims from inside the industry have intensified scrutiny of AI development, prompting Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to call for the pace of AI development to slow, external and urge governments to regulate the industry. The post was applauded by Altman, Google's DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk. By Tuesday, however, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement. Altman said AI companies were capable of regulating themselves. "We will get it right," Altman said, adding that if firms could not keep "alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" they would "slow down or stop". But Yoshua Bengio, one of the pioneers of modern AI, posted on X, external "ambitious efforts outside the for-profit sector" were needed to "avert the worst risks from AI". - Why doomsday warnings are not the only threat to the AI juggernaut - Published21 hours ago Some industry figures have argued resurgent AI fears were overblown and were being jumped on to generate hype for the industry. During the conference, Altman addressed a crowd of hundreds of business people, telling them they should use AI tools to aid in their work, but also needed them in order to protect their businesses from potentially AI-enabled cyber attacks. The idea of AI executives being left to entirely regulate themselves has struck some in the industry as a bad idea. Jack Clark, an Anthropic executive and co-founder, told the BBC on Monday that leaving AI to be a "totally unregulated industry" was "rolling dice with immense risks". Patrick Hillman, the chief operating officer of Logical Intelligence, which is chaired by Yann LeCun, a sage of the AI industry, noted Tuesday how little faith people have in tech companies to do anything truly in the public interest, external. "The only institution that Americans might trust less than Washington these days is Silicon Valley. I have worked and lived in both and I assure you both have earned this scepticism," Hillman said. "If you believe what you are building is dangerous, show us what you are prepared to stop doing," he added. Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety. Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development. He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact. "We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said. OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind. "With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote. item.title: Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over future
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6dj4nn0n97ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over future - Published The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future. The premiers - all of whom are part of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) - wrote that restoring trust in their party lay in "listening and taking political action, not in debates over personnel". Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months, is facing poor approval ratings while the anti-immigration, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is surging, prompting questions about whether he is an electoral liability. He has vowed to carry on but two more state elections on Sunday have been seen as a key test of his leadership. Rumours of a "Kanzlertausch" - or "Chancellor swap" - have been around for months, but they have increased since the conservative CDU tumbled to a distant second behind the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt at the start of September. The AfD shot up to 43.8% of the vote while the CDU plummeted to 17.2%, marking the first time since World War Two that a far-right party has come close to controlling a German state. It is still three seats short of an outright majority and the major parties would not enter into a coalition with the AfD, though it could seek to form a minority government. Merz came out fighting after the loss, describing the AfD - which wants to rebuild ties with Russia - as a "destructive force" whose migration policy amounted to an "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers. The AfD responded to his remarks by saying it was filing a defamation complaint against the chancellor over what it described as "baseless" and "disgusting" claims. The chancellor's abrasive communication style and personal unpopularity - with just 14% thinking he is right for the job, according to a recent Bild poll - have raised questions about his viability as leader of both Germany and the CDU. The CDU's eight state premiers wrote, however, that "now more than ever, Germany's political landscape needs stability". "Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag [German parliament]," said the leaders of Schleswig-Holstein, Saxony, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia. - How significant are AfD's historic gains for Germany and the rest of Europe? - Published7 September It comes after Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria and leader of the CDU's sister party the CSU, stood by Merz. An unnamed party source told news agency Reuters that CDU officials will meet on Sunday to co-ordinate the party's response to the results of that day's state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania - where the AfD is poised for further gains and the CDU for further losses. However, the race is far more evenly split in the German capital than it was in Saxony-Anhalt, with the CDU and Die Linke (The Left) vying for first place, and the AfD and Greens not far behind, according to polls. In Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, polls put the AfD ahead of the centre-left SPD but likely well short of an outright majority. The worst-case scenario for Merz would be for the CDU to lose power in Berlin and not get enough votes to even have a presence in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania's parliament. Unlike in the UK, Germany is not well-versed in replacing its leader mid-term, though Merz could, in theory, be pressured to resign or face a vote of no confidence, though many regard that outcome as unlikely. No one within the CDU has yet said they were willing to challenge Merz, but the speculation about his future has led to several names - including Söder, North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik Wüst and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt - being touted as potential successors. Even before Merz had officially been made chancellor, he managed to rally support for a massive €500bn ($547bn; £420bn) defence infrastructure fund, with his straight-talking style and focus on European security earning him plaudits on the world stage. But it took him three attempts to become CDU leader and he then lost an initial vote to become chancellor despite technically having sufficient votes through a coalition deal with the SPD. It was a first in post-war Germany. This suggests that he has a history of struggling to appeal to even those within his own ranks - and that he may be unlikely to let go of a job he has long coveted. - Published7 days ago - Published7 September

item.title: Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr89jqd1w45eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Saudi Arabia says it shot down Houthi drone south of Mecca - Published Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen. Turki al-Maliki said the targeting of Mecca, which is the home of Islam's most sacred shrine and the focal point of the Hajj pilgrimage, was a "disgraceful act". The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression". But the Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of western Yemen, denied targeting Mecca and accused Saudi Arabia of "fabrications and lies". "There is no threat whatsoever from Yemen to the holy sites. Our operations target their oil facilities and military bases, and are far removed from the holy places," military spokesman Yahya Sarea said. Sarea added that the Houthis had launched drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia in retaliation for more than 450 Saudi air strikes on their territory over the past week. He also said they had shot down a Saudi fighter jet over Marib province. There was no immediate response from the Saudi-led coalition, but Maj Gen Maliki did say that its forces would "not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia and its hostile and terrorist behaviour". On Tuesday, Saudi authorities issued a series of brief security alerts for incoming projectiles in a number of western areas, including Mecca and Jeddah, the kingdom's second largest city. Meanwhile, the US embassy in Saudi Arabia issued a "reconsider travel" advisory, warning that Houthi attacks had targeted cities, infrastructure, airports, military bases, diplomatic facilities and energy facilities. The Houthis have recently seized control of large swathes of Yemen's Red Sea coast from Saudi-backed pro-government forces. Last week, they captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a key shipping route that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and the Suez canal. The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf. At the same time, Saudi Arabia's key East-West Pipeline, which was being used to transfer crude oil from the Gulf to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, had to be closed after it was badly damaged in a strike that the kingdom blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq. Some experts have said it could take more than a month to repair the pipeline, but US Energy Secretary Chris Wright predicted on Tuesday that oil should be flowing through it within days. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the country's de facto ruler, has personally pressed US President Donald Trump to take military action against the Houthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. Trump has so far declined to involve the US military directly, offering instead to assist with intelligence and targeting support, the sources said. A senior Trump administration official told the BBC: "We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability." The United Nations Security Council held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, during which both Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia called for more decisive action against the Houthis, who they accused of choking the Bab al-Mandab Strait as a way of applying economic pressure. Council members agreed that freedom of navigation in the Red Sea must be maintained to prevent disruption to global supply chains. More than 90,000 people have been displaced in Yemen by the fighting between the Houthis and pro-government forces, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). "Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left," Amy Pope, the IOM's director general, warned last week. The World Health Organization (WHO) said on Sunday that at least 500 people had been reported killed since the start of August, including 297 over the previous week. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. The fighting has reportedly left more than 150,000 people dead and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with more than 22 million people in need of some form of aid, according to the UN. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

item.title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his shooting
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzrz4xmknjgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Charlie Kirk's family alleges 'stunning failures' by Utah officials led to his shooting - Published Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event. In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target. Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof. The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News. "We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community." The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit. It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him. "Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges. "Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says. Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site. The family also alleges the university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking. "The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing. Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial. Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges. Prosecutors have called for the death penalty.

item.title: Journalist and pilot among three killed after news helicopter crashes in LA
item.description:

========================================
Journalist and pilot among three killed after news helicopter crashes in LA - Published Photojournalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw have been named as being among three people killed after an NBC Los Angeles helicopter crashed in the city's suburbs, the station has confirmed. NBC Los Angeles said its NewsChopper4, which also operated for Telemundo 52, was in the area on Tuesday reporting on a deadly bus crash which killed two people. Fire officials said an unidentified pedestrian was also killed, and two others were taken to hospital. Tributes, including from the local news community, have started to come in led by the station's hosts, who called the victims "valued friends and colleagues". One CBS editor said their "hearts are shattered". "That helicopter community is a small group of people, and it's just devastating to know that this has happened to one of those people, to our friends and our colleagues at NBC4," said Mike Rogers, CBS Los Angeles assignment editor. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said she was "absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight". "My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash," she wrote on X, while the Los Angeles Fire Department (LAFD) similarly extended its "thoughts and prayers" to all those affected. The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time (01:00 BST) between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighbourhood, an LAFD spokesperson told the BBC. Fire from the crash spread to four vehicles and two storage containers, and more than 70 firefighters were deployed to the scene, the LAFD added. During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed it was the local news station's helicopter that crashed. "We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation," Williams said. Earlier, LAFD Captain Branden Silverman told the local affiliate of the BBC's US partner CBS that the third victim in the crash appeared to have been on the ground. "That person was declared deceased on scene," Silverman said. Several news helicopters were in the area at the time of the incident reporting on a bus crash. In the crash which was being reported on, two people were killed and six others were injured when an SUV hit a city bus in Chatsworth, BBC's US partner CBS reported. California Governor Gavin Newsom wrote on X that "our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family". "Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight." The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) will lead the investigation into the incident.

item.title: Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6kgxjl35822o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Colombia and Brazil deadliest countries for environmental activists, report says - Published Colombia has again topped the list of countries with the highest number of killings of land and environmental activists, according to an annual report by campaign group Global Witness, external. Out of at least 124 activists killed globally in 2025, 39 were murdered in Colombia, followed by Brazil with 26. Global Witness says that 85% of the documented killings took place in Latin America, making it the deadliest region for every year since the group started publishing its reports in 2012. Most of the killings were part of land disputes and in many cases they were carried out by hitmen or members of organised crime gangs, the report states. Colombia has accounted for the highest number of murders of environmental activists for the past four years. Almost half of those killed in the country were members of indigenous groups, while many of the remaining ones were small-scale farmers, Global Witness's report says. Many indigenous groups in Colombia have created their own protection networks in the form of indigenous guards, which patrol their territory but are unarmed. Members of indigenous guards are often targeted by illegal armed groups looking to expand their territory to plant coca - the raw material used to make cocaine - or to engage in illegal mining. Last week, Jacob Guachetá Zambrano, who was part of the indigenous guard in Colombia's Cauca region, was found tortured and killed. While the possible motive behind his murder is still under investigation and the search for the perpetrator is ongoing, indigenous leaders said that murders, threats and forced disappearances in the area were common as illegal armed groups battled for territory. Global Witness warned that Brazil had seen a doubling of killings of environmental defenders in 2025 compared to 2024. As in Colombia, in Brazil most of the cases the group documented were primarily driven by conflict over land, Global Witness's researchers found. Outside of Latin America, 12% of the murders occurred in Asia, with Philippines top of the list with 12 documented murders. The group warned that while globally the number of documented killings had gone down from 146 in 2024 to 128 in 2025, its numbers were probably an underestimate as many cases went unreported. item.title: US limits visas for South African officials over alleged anti-white discrimination
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqy0z5y7wnp2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US limits visas for South African officials over alleged anti-white discrimination - Published The US has announced visa restrictions targeting people it accuses of discriminating against South Africa's white minority, in the latest escalation of tensions between the two countries. The Trump administration has criticised South Africa over several issues, including policies aimed at addressing racial inequality that it says discriminate against Afrikaners, descendants mainly of Dutch and French settlers. South Africa has repeatedly denied the claim. South Africa's Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said he noted the announcement with "concern". "The announcement once again, [sic] aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa's domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of 'minorities' and Afrikaners in general," said a statement from the international relations and co-operation ministry. Announcing the restrictions on Tuesday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said: "The South African government has not adequately addressed the previously laid out concerns." He said the visa restrictions would target those who promote "race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa." Rubio did not immediately name any individuals targeted by the restrictions. - Ramaphosa struggles to mend fences with Trump - Published17 July 2025 - Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? - Published2 June 2025 Relations between the two countries have been on a downward spiral since President Donald Trump returned to office early last year, with the US leader cutting aid, expelling the South African ambassador and offering "refuge" to white South Africans fleeing "persecution." The South African government has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is persecuting white people or confiscating their land. It said claims of a white genocide had been widely discredited and lacked reliable evidence. South Africa's latest crime statistics do not indicate that white people are at a greater risk of violent crime than other racial groups. Trump offered refugee status to Afrikaners last year after South African President Cyril Ramaphosa signed a law allowing the government to seize land without compensation in rare instances. The legislation allows the state to expropriate property in the public interest and provides for circumstances in which compensation may be set at zero. But it also requires authorities, in most cases, to first try to reach an agreement with property owners, and disputes can be taken to court. Land ownership remains a highly sensitive issue in South Africa more than three decades after the end of apartheid, under which the black majority was dispossessed of land and denied many basic rights. The government says land reform is necessary to address those historic inequalities and insists the new law does not permit arbitrary seizures. Most private farmland is owned by white South Africans, who make up just over 7% of the population. In Wednesday's statement, South Africa's government said: "It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation's concern over centuries of racial injustice." In a separate social media post on Tuesday, Rubio accused South Africa's government of pursuing "racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority" and said those responsible for what he described as injustices "have no place in the United States". He said the South African government had failed to adequately address US concerns about what Washington describes as "government-sponsored discrimination" against Afrikaners and other minorities. "The United States will not allow such behaviour to go unchecked," he added. He said the actions targeted by the policy undermined "peace, economic stability and the rule of law." The US embassy in Pretoria said Washington believed dialogue with South Africa had run its course and accused the African country of failing to demonstrate a commitment to strong bilateral relations. It warned that the new visa restrictions were the beginning of tougher measures, adding: "This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America's firm resolve in this matter." South Africa made efforts to soothe tensions with US, with Ramaphosa going to the White House in May last year with a large delegation that included white members of his coalition government and also famous white South African golfers. But Trump ambushed the Oval Office meeting with claims that white South African farmers were being killed and "persecuted" - producing unsubstantiated evidence that has been widely discredited. Further efforts by South Africa to mend the relationship have failed, with Africa's largest economy being hit in August with 30% tariffs on goods being exported to the US - the highest rate in sub-Saharan Africa. The latest visa restrictions are being imposed under a provision of US immigration law that allows the secretary of state to bar foreign nationals whose entry is considered potentially damaging to US foreign policy interests. item.title: Philippines' Duterte seen in person at International Criminal Court for first time
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq986j7x1nd3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Philippines' Duterte seen in person at International Criminal Court for first time - Published Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte has appeared in person at the International Criminal Court in The Hague, where he is due to be tried for alleged crimes against humanity. He is facing charges over his bloody war on drugs, which saw tens of thousands of small-time drug dealers allegedly executed summarily. The 81-year-old wore a dark suit and white shirt on Wednesday, which marked the first time he has been seen in person since his arrest in Manila 18 months ago. He did not speak but waved at family members in the public gallery when proceedings ended. Until now he had appeared before the court by video link and then skipped multiple hearings. The ICC called a status hearing on Wednesday after Duterte's lawyers argued the former leader's deteriorating health had made him unfit to stand trial . The first trial date is scheduled for 30 November. The war on drugs was the centrepiece of Duterte's presidency, which ran from 2016 to 2022. He argued peace and order was necessary to grow the economy. The ICC is looking at killings from 1 November 2011, when Duterte was mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, until 16 March 2019, when he withdrew the Philippines' membership in the ICC. Duterte's lawyer Peter Haynes recently told the court his client was suffering from "significant memory impairment", making him unable to engage with his legal team. Prosecutors argued otherwise. Judges are deliberating whether Duterte is mentally fit to be tried and have ordered a medical assessment by three specialists. That assessment has not been made public but according to AFP, defence lawyers say it shows Duterte thinks he is living in 2007 or 2008, that he is 84 or 85 years old, and was found to be unable to recall Donald Trump's name. Relatives of those killed in Duterte's brutal anti-drugs campaign watched the proceedings over a livestream in Manila. Llore Pasco, who lost two sons, told Reuters: "We're happy that he has finally appeared and that he looks OK. In fact, he looks like he has put on weight." Randy Delos Santos, who lost his teenage nephew in 2017, told AFP he was happy to see Duterte in court, adding: "We hope that his being physically fit will help speed up the hearings." In 2019, when he was still president, Duterte revealed he was suffering from myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune condition that causes nerve malfunction. At 71 in 2016, he was the oldest Philippine president at the time of election. Duterte's family is currently caught in a high-stakes dynasty war for control of the Philippines. His daughter, Vice-President Sara Duterte, has feuded spectacularly with President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos. The break-up of the Duterte-Marcos alliance, which helped them win the 2022 elections by a landslide, paved the way for the Rodrigo Duterte's arrest at Manila airport in March 2025. Sara Duterte is a frontrunner to replace Marcos in the 2028 elections, where the incumbent is ineligible under the constitution to stand for a second term. But she is also fighting for her political survival in an impeachment trial, where if convicted, she will be disqualified from running for public office. She is charged with misusing public funds and threatening to have Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and Marcos' cousin, congressman Ferdinand Martin Romualdez assassinated. item.title: Legendary Nigerian actor Olu Jacobs dies aged 84
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4gr5jnd134o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Legendary Nigerian actor Olu Jacobs dies aged 84 - Published Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84. His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns. Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought". Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day. He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country. "We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement. Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films. He became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility. His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours. In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry. Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria. In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health. In 2021, Silva disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Dementia with Lewy bodies. "It's a degenerative disease that affects the brain and it's almost like a Parkinson-type of disease - it affects the brain and affects the person," she said in an interview with Nigerian broadcaster Chude Jideonwo. On several occasions, there were rumours that Jacobs had died, but his family would promptly debunk them, the latest being in June 2024 when his eldest son, Soji, went on TV to say his father was still alive. item.title: Tall athletes can't stretch their legs in container beds at Asian Games, official says
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c620lg854v45o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Tall athletes can't stretch their legs in container beds at Asian Games, official says - Published Wooden container huts meant for thousands of athletes have become the subject of heated criticism ahead of the opening of Japan's Asian Games on Saturday. Jung Jae-yong, vice-president of the Korea Basketball Association, told AFP news agency the accommodation was the "worst it has ever been". "Athletes who are over two metres (6ft 7in) tall cannot even stretch their legs out on the beds. It's unreasonable." The Games, held in the city of Nagoya and wider Aichi prefecture, have faced weeks of concern about a potential shortage of beds. More than 17,000 athletes and officials are attending - exceeding the initial 15,000 expected. The containers, which will be housing around 2,000 of the guests and are designed to be reused as disaster evacuation facilities, have been beset by complaints. A member of the South Korea basketball team posted a video of a leaking pipe and soaked floor in his room, with the caption: "Please help me." Athletes were also briefly evacuated from the containers as record rainfall lashed Nagoya last week and caused widespread flooding. Water leakage was reported in some of the competition venues too. Jung, the basketball official, told AFP that concerns over accommodation were shared by representatives from the other countries at the Games. Indian authorities have built replicas of the huts to get their athletes used to living in them. Accommodation manager Yuta Matsuo told Reuters the hosts were "fully aware of the dissatisfaction and concerns voiced by the athlete delegations". They were "taking concrete steps to improve the environment for the athletes", he said. Unlike the Olympic Games, where there is usually a designated athletes' village, organisers have opted to use temporary accommodation for competitors. Beyond the container huts, between 4,000 and 5,000 participants will be staying on an Italian cruise ship which docked in Nagoya on Tuesday. The rest of the attendees will stay in hotels. Initially, 15,000 athletes and officials had been expected to attend the Games. But in mid-August the Olympic Council of Asia said the number would be closer to 17,000 after teqball - which combines elements of football and table tennis - and padel were included. Hideaki Omura, president of the organising committee and Governor of Aichi Prefecture, previously said authorities had set aside a budget for 15,000 people and had "neither the manpower nor the budget to make the necessary arrangements" for the additional athletes. "There is simply nowhere for them to stay. If they still wish to come, they will have to make their own arrangements." But last month, organisers and the Olympic Council of Asia said all "17,000-plus" athletes and officials who had registered before the deadline in July have been provided with "Games-appropriate accommodation". "The final preparations are all on track and progressing smoothly ahead of what promises to be the most spectacular Asian Games held for generations," their statement read. Philippine Olympic Committee president Abraham Tolentino told AFP that while all the country's athletes have secured a bed, some officials and coaches were staying in "different hotels and Airbnb". Though basketball and football matches have already started, the Asian Games officially begin on Saturday and will end on 4 October. - Published28 August - Published1 day ago

item.title: Lost on Mount Fuji off-season? You'll have to pay for your rescue
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r6mvjdvedo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lost on Mount Fuji off-season? You'll have to pay for your rescue - Published From next year, people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service, authorities governing the northern part of the peak say. The fee is among a series of measures Japan's Yamanashi prefecture is introducing to deter reckless and poorly prepared climbers. A similar fee of 8,000 yen ($51; £38) per five minutes is already in place in nearby Saitama prefecture for other mountainous areas and will be used as a reference. Yamanashi authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season, which runs from early September to July the following year, to submit detailed climbing plans. "We ask the general public to refrain from climbing during the off-season. We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Yamanashi Governor Kotaro Nagasaki said on Monday. Officials in Yamanashi and neighbouring Shizuoka prefecture, which governs the southern part of Fuji, have seen a rise in off-season and unplanned climbs, some of which have left climbers stranded. Shizuoka authorities say they will impose penalties on people who fail to register their off-season climbing attempts and strengthen efforts to keep climbers out of restricted areas. They did not announce a helicopter rescue fee. Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from July to early September, with about 200,000 hikers attempting the summit each year. Climbing outside of those months is highly discouraged although permitted up to the fifth of ten stations. However, most mountain huts and toilet facilities are closed off season. The weather and trail conditions also tend to be more severe.

item.title: Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8ly49w9g1edo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Suspected sabotage causes major Netherlands rail disruption - Published Parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, were hit by major rail disruption after suspected sabotage to the tracks on Tuesday morning, the country's railway infrastructure operator said. ProRail said pipes and cables were laid on tracks at multiple locations in the country's centre and north in more than 35 incidents. It added the acts appeared to be intentional, causing widespread cancellations and delays, with new disruptions occurring in some places after objects had initially been removed. No suspects or motives have yet been identified. Police said a criminal investigation had been launched. The operator said the pipes and cables caused its computer systems to believe trains were on the tracks, meaning traffic control was unable to clear the railway. "Placing materials on the tracks is extremely dangerous and unacceptable, and fortunately, it did not lead to any accidents today," it said. Speaking earlier, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten described the incidents as "disruptive and life-threatening". In one case early on Monday, a train "struck metal" on the track near Steenwijk, in the country's east. ProRail said there was no further damage because the train was not travelling at full speed. The national public prosecutor's office and the Netherlands' intelligence agency AIVD are investigating the incident alongside police. Routes to the main international airport, Schiphol, Eindhoven and Utrecht were among those affected on Tuesday. The closure of some level crossings also caused some disruption to roads. As of about 17:00 CEST (16:00 GMT), it said no new blockages had been reported since 13:00, with current ones now resolved. Train operator Nederlandse Spoorwegen (NS) still showed disruptions to two lines on Tuesday evening. Its interim CEO Mirjam van Velthuizen said the events had highlighted the Netherlands' dependence on the railway and called for investment in contingency planning. "In a world where uncertainties are increasing, we must ensure that the railway can absorb disruptions, that the impact remains limited as much as possible, and that we can recover as quickly as possible," she said. NS earlier said that disruption was so extensive it was "not possible" to provide a bus replacement service. Netherlands Police said units from across the country were investigating Tuesday's events. Tuesday is Prinsjesdag in the Netherlands - the day the government presents its budget. Hay bales were lit on fire along various roads across the Netherlands in the afternoon, after Farmers Defence Force (FDF) - a group aimed at defending the interests of Dutch farmers and farm workers - said protests would take place. The group is opposing government plans asking them to reduce nitrogen emissions. Authorities have not established a link between the protests and the disruption on the rail network. The FDF said it was not responsible for the railway sabotage, but said it could not rule out the involvement of individual farmers. Disruption in the Netherlands came after separate reports in French media suggested a derailment in Normandy on Friday could have been an act of sabotage. According to prosecutors, a section of rail found on the track may have caused the crash. But France's interior minister Laurent Nunez has urged caution while an investigation is ongoing, saying that authorities are pursuing all leads.

item.title: Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65yw2gq2nrno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Satellite image reveals major damage that shut crucial Saudi oil pipeline - Published Satellite imagery shows a key oil pipeline in Saudi Arabia has been badly damaged after a strike last week, which experts have told BBC Verify could take more than a month to repair and force oil prices even higher. The image shows the most significant damage is at a pumping station along the East-West Pipeline, which Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on to export crude oil via the Red Sea rather than through the Strait of Hormuz, where ships have been attacked by Iran and the US during their six-month war. The Saudi government has accused Iranian-backed militias in Iraq of the pipeline strike, which followed days of renewed missile and drone attacks on south-western Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthi group - which is also backed by Iran. Saudi Arabia has retaliated by carrying out strikes on Houthi-controlled areas of western Yemen. New satellite images also show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base after a Houthi strike last week. The Saudi government said on Tuesday it would respond "firmly" to attacks by the Houthis. While the Houthis have been fighting a long-running civil war against Saudi-backed Yemeni pro-government forces, the group has stepped up its campaign in recent weeks. It seized control of significant new territory across Yemen's south-western coast last week, including areas overlooking the crucial Bab al-Mandab waterway, strengthening its ability to enforce its declared blockade of Saudi shipping. The price of a barrel of oil has surged since Saudi Arabia said on Friday it was closing the pipeline as a precaution. Brent crude was trading as high as $108 (£80) a barrel on Tuesday, down slightly from $109.80 on Monday. Experts from trade intelligence firm Kpler said the pipeline's closure could reduce oil supplies by as much as 3.6 million barrels per day - or about 3.6% of global demand. "Based on new information we've received, damage to the pipeline could take four to six weeks to resolve, given spare-parts availability and impaired supply chains," said Homayoun Falakshahi, Kpler's head of crude oil analysis. Anne-Sophie Corbeau, from the Center on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University, said pipelines are "like sitting ducks" and recent strikes are a "very important signal" indicating workarounds being used to avoid the Strait of Hormuz "may not be super useful because they can be destroyed". The Houthis have targeted other Saudi oil infrastructure with drones and missiles which has led to some operations being suspended. There have also been attacks on military bases. New satellite images captured on Monday show damage to Saudi Arabia's King Khalid Air Base near Khamis Mushait which the Houthis said they had targeted with ballistic missiles and drones last week after it was used to carry out air strikes on Yemen. At least three aircraft hangars or shelters appear to have been damaged at the Royal Saudi Air Force facility where US-made F-15 fighter jets are based. The Saudi-led anti-Houthi military coalition of Arab states said on Tuesday that a Houthi missile and drone attack had injured 13 people in attacks on what the coalition said were "civilian objects". The Houthis said Saudi Arabia had carried out with more than 50 strikes in western Yemen over the previous 24 hours. The UN Refugee Agency has said that more than 100,000 people have been internally displaced by the renewed conflict. Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler and Benedict Garman Graphics by Tom Shiel

item.title: What weapon could the US have put into space?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4zqgk97wlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What weapon could the US have put into space? - Published The announcement by the United States that it has deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit has raised questions about what weaponry is actually in space, and what role it could play in efforts by great powers to dominate that arena. Washington has given away little in its announcement. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit. So what could this weapon be, and what is the wider picture like for military developments in space? Who else could have similar weaponry? Space has been a militarised domain since the start of the space age - in the late 1960s, the Soviet Union deployed weapons up there. The Istrebitel Sputnikov (IS; Satellite Destroyer) programme was made up of satellites that were designed to release projectiles that detonated, releasing shrapnel into the path of another (usually American) satellite. Nowadays, advanced militaries deploy satellites in space for a range of purposes, including reconnaissance, secure communications, detecting missile launches and providing precise location information for targeted strikes. As warfare becomes more technologically advanced, analysts expect the use of military hardware in space to increase. Dr Bleddyn Bowen, an associate fellow in military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute and associate professor in astropolitics at Durham University, said he was only able to hazard a guess about the weapon announced by the US. "I would expect there to be some kind of electronic warfare or radio-jamming platform, possibly, this would be a non-destructive kind of anti-satellite weapon," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme. Such weaponry already exists on Earth and can disrupt satellite communications, he said. "If you take out the radio links then your satellite is very useless." Bowen also would not rule out a riskier and more disruptive type of weaponry, which could create debris and destruction. "Less likely would be a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort, so a vehicle that would release a projectile that could ram into a satellite and destroy it," he said. A type of "close inspection and grappling satellite would be another possibility as well." As to whether rivals such as Russia and China have similar weaponry already in orbit, is difficult to tell. "If we're looking towards China and Russia, they have both displayed activity," Juliana Suess, a former research fellow at RUSI and researcher at the Stiftung Wissenschaft und Politik (German Institute for International and Security Affairs), told the BBC. "For example, with Russia, we've seen some activity that hints at being a co-orbital weapons test. So we saw something that might indicate that they shot a projectile as a test in orbit. "There are others out there, but without knowing the details, what the American [weapon] is, it's difficult to draw comparisons." But while the weapon placed in orbit may be unusual, the US - and indeed its Russian and Chinese rivals - have had weapons that can be pointed and shot into space for some time. In a later BBC interview, Bowen was dismissive of China's reaction to the US announcement which warned against an arms race in space, describing it as "the pot calling the kettle black". "If you're already an expert... you know how hollow those words are coming from the Russian and Chinese governments," he said. "The United States, Russia and China and also India have all developed different kinds of anti-satellite or counter-space weapons, and Russia and China have put a lot of technologies in space which have a lot of weapons potential," he added. In fact in the past 10 years, Russia and China have been doing a lot more manoeuvres in space, known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs) - "buzzing" Western satellites. "Theoretically, these RPO [satellites]can become hunter-killer satellites by physically colliding with them or by nudging them out of orbit," Dr Rod Thornton, reader in Russian Defence and Security Studies at King's College, London, told the BBC. Bowen added that the Chinese have demonstrated "space tug capability", saying: "A vehicle can go up to a satellite, can grapple it and move it into a different orbit." This, he said, could be a positive development - a way of removing space junk as well as knocking out working satellites. However, some types of space weaponry also have the potential to create huge amounts of space junk. Dr Mark Hilborne, a specialist in space security and weaponisation at King's College, said direct ascent anti-satellite missile tests, such as one carried out by China in 2007, leave a great deal of debris in orbit for a very long time. Suess said debris from that test was still in orbit and still dangerous. "It doesn't have to be a sort of huge piece of metal to do any damage, it can be a tiny piece of plastic, given the velocity that we're talking about in orbit," she said. The nuclear threat Thornton said that what Russia lacks in space weaponry and satellites, it makes up for in missile capability. "The Russians... have ground-based missiles which can be launched into space to strike [satellites] in low Earth orbit. They also have ASAT [air-launched antisatellite] missiles that can be launched from a great height by aircraft," he said. "From the Russian point of view, they see Nato as having much better and more satellites than the Russian military can call up, therefore they have invested heavily in ASATs in order to 'level the battlefield' somewhat." Thornton added a sobering thought: "As a last resort, the Russians can also launch nuclear weapons into space and the EMP [nuclear electromagnetic pulse] blast would 'fry' any unhardened satellite over a wide expanse." So what is the likelihood of a nuclear conflict in space? Only if it was happening on the ground as well. "What could happen in space is not something that would happen in isolation, really," Bowen said. "Nothing could happen, or something could." Given that weapons for use in space have been around for so long, why did the US announcement come when it did? Experts agree that it's not a major development as such, more a political signal. Bowen suggested that it could be a response to Chinese developments. "China has modernised its military forces over the past 30 years," he said. "It has put a lot more military satellites in space and has presented a lot more targets that are worth the American military going after and hitting." "There's much more incentive for American space weapons now because China has a lot of vulnerability to space in the same way that the Americans have." This situation seems to have created a curious imbalance. Thornton said that, Russia would be the "big winner" in any space war, because it has so few satellites, unlike China and the US. It would involve "missiles fired up into space, manoeuvring satellites designed to nudge/destroy them and ground-based lasers," he said.
